target.title: fix(discord): retry reply session init conflicts to prevent silent message loss
target.body:
Closes #102381

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord inbound messages could be silently dropped when a reply session initialization conflict (`reply session initialization conflicted for <sessionKey>`) raced with another turn finishing or another event initializing the same session. Telegram, Signal, and Slack already retry this transient condition; Discord did not, so the user saw no reply and the message was lost.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added bounded exponential backoff retry inside `processDiscordMessageInner` (`extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.ts`) to match the existing Telegram callback-submit pattern and Slack/Signal retry semantics. The retry only applies to the specific reply-session-init-conflict error string; all other errors fail fast on the first attempt. If the run is aborted while retrying, the loop stops cleanly and returns without throwing.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:** the retry boundary was narrowed so context/history preparation runs exactly once and only the dispatch/session-init attempt is retried. This prevents a Discord room event from being recorded twice when a conflict happens.

## User Impact

Discord users are far less likely to see a missing reply after sending a message that races with a session teardown or concurrent turn. Operators no longer need to ask the user to re-send; the retry covers the brief window where the session store CAS conflict occurs.

## Evidence

- Added a focused regression test suite in `extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts`:
  - retries with exponential backoff until dispatch succeeds (250 ms, 1000 ms, 2500 ms)
  - throws the last error after exhausting retries
  - does not retry unrelated dispatch errors
  - stops retrying when the abort signal fires
  - **records room event history exactly once across conflict retries** (new regression test for the narrowed boundary)

target.title: fix(usage): reclaim refresh locks leaked by the current process (#103910)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw gateway usage-cost` can get stuck with `cacheStatus.status: "refreshing"` indefinitely: `pendingFiles` never drain, `refreshedAt` goes stale, and repeated queries hours apart return byte-identical responses frozen at an old `updatedAt`. Root cause: usage-cost refreshes serialize on a pid-stamped lock file (`.usage-cost-cache.json.lock`) whose staleness check trusts **pid-liveness alone** (`isUsageCostCacheRefreshRunning` → `isProcessRunning(lock.pid)`). A lock leaked by the gateway's **own process** — e.g. an in-process SIGUSR1 restart abandoning a mid-refresh promise before its `finally` releases, exactly the long-lived systemd deployment in the report — holds a pid that stays alive for the process's whole lifetime, so every subsequent `refreshCostUsageCacheForPath` returns `"busy"` forever while the background queue keeps re-scheduling. Fixes #103910.

## Why This Change Was Made

Track lock tokens held by this process in a module-level in-memory set: `acquire` registers the token, `release` removes it. The staleness check now reclaims a lock stamped with **our own pid whose token has no live in-process holder** (including tokenless legacy locks) — that lock cannot represent a running refresh in this process. Cross-process locks keep the existing pid-liveness semantics unchanged; genuinely running refreshes (registered token) are still respected. No new options or public surface.

## User Impact

`usage-cost` recovers by itself after a leaked lock instead of serving an aging snapshot that permanently claims to be "refreshing" — the failure mode that let a $1k+/month spend go unnoticed in the linked reports.

## Evidence

Discriminating regression test — forge a lock with `pid: process.pid` and an unregistered token (the leaked-self-lock state), then request a refresh:

```
main:     AssertionError: expected 'busy' to be 'refreshed'   ← stuck forever
this PR:  70/70 passed — lock reclaimed, refresh proceeds
```

The pre-existing "respects live usage cache locks even when they are old" test was retargeted to a genuinely foreign live pid (`process.ppid`), preserving its original intent under the new same-pid contract. Full suite `session-cost-usage.test.ts` 70/70; `tsgo:core` 0 errors; `oxfmt`/`oxlint` clean.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `openclaw googlemeet join --mode transcribe` (and `googlemeet.create`) with the Chrome transport would silently fail when an existing Meet tab was rendered in a non-English UI. The plugin's browser automation matches English aria-labels and page text ("Join now", "Turn off microphone", etc.), so a reused tab opened in Japanese or another locale would never reach `inCall: true`, enable captions, or return a meeting URL, with no error pointing at the UI language.

If the tab is already using English UI, the URL is unchanged and no navigation is issued.

## User Impact

Users with Google accounts or browser profiles that default Meet to a non-English language can now rely on `googlemeet join`/`create` with the Chrome transport without manually appending `?hl=en` to the URL. Join/status behavior becomes language-independent for reused tabs.

target.title: fix(gateway): bound busy channel health by real run age
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`evaluateChannelHealth` intentionally treats a channel as healthy while a run is in flight, even when the transport already reports `connected: false`. That busy override is meant to be bounded by a 25 minute stale ceiling, but the ceiling is measured from `lastRunActivityAt`, which the run-state heartbeat refreshes every 60 seconds for as long as any run is active.

If a per-message task hangs forever, for example a channel send blocking on a half-open or dead socket with no send timeout after the transport disconnected, `onRunEnd` never fires, the heartbeat keeps ticking, and `lastRunActivityAt` never ages past roughly 60 seconds. The `>= 25min` stuck branch, the only escape from busy-overrides-disconnected, becomes permanently unreachable. The account is then reported healthy forever by the channel health monitor (`if (health.healthy) continue`), the readiness probe (`src/gateway/server/readiness.ts`), and the `openclaw health` CLI (`src/commands/health.ts`). No restart fires and no operator-visible signal appears until the process is restarted. Transport disconnects mid-send with no send timeout are a normal production failure mode.

## Why This Change Was Made

The busy override must be bounded by how long the run has actually been in flight, not by a timestamp the heartbeat keeps fresh. A single hung run must eventually breach the stale ceiling.

Root cause, `src/gateway/channel-health-policy.ts` busy branch (before):

```ts
const runActivityAge =
  lastRunActivityAt == null
    ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
    : Math.max(0, policy.now - lastRunActivityAt);
if (runActivityAge < BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS) {
  return { healthy: true, reason: "busy" };
}
return { healthy: false, reason: "stuck" };
```

`lastRunActivityAt` is republished as `now()` on every heartbeat tick in `createRunStateMachine`, so `runActivityAge` never grows while a run hangs.

Fix. `createRunStateMachine` now tracks each in-flight run's start time keyed by an opaque run handle returned from `onRunStart` and passed back to `onRunEnd`, and publishes the oldest still-active run's start as `activeRunStartedAt`. When the oldest run ends the reported start advances to the next-oldest, and it clears when no run is active. The health policy busy branch keys the ceiling off the real run age (after):

```ts
const runStartAge =
  activeRunStartedAt == null ? null : Math.max(0, policy.now - activeRunStartedAt);
const runActivityAge =
  lastRunActivityAt == null ? null : Math.max(0, policy.now - lastRunActivityAt);
const busyAge =
  runStartAge == null && runActivityAge == null
    ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
    : Math.max(runStartAge ?? 0, runActivityAge ?? 0);
if (busyAge < BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS) {
  return { healthy: true, reason: "busy" };
}
return { healthy: false, reason: "stuck" };
```

Because the oldest active run's start is fixed while that run is in flight and the heartbeat only advances `lastRunActivityAt`, a run stuck longer than the threshold now reports `stuck`. Because the reported start is the oldest active run and advances as runs complete, a channel churning through many short overlapping runs stays healthy; only a genuinely hung run breaches the ceiling. The `activeRunStartedAt` field flows through the same run-state to snapshot path as `lastRunActivityAt` (`run-state-machine.ts` publish, `account-snapshot-fields.ts` read, `types.core.ts` snapshot type), so all three consumers of `evaluateChannelHealth` (monitor, readiness, CLI) get the corrected verdict.

## Why This Is The Right Boundary

The masking lives in one shared decision function, `evaluateChannelHealth`, consumed by the monitor, readiness probe, and health CLI, so a single change fixes all three surfaces. The heartbeat that defeats the ceiling lives in `createRunStateMachine`, the one owner of run activity status, so the run-age fact is surfaced where it is produced rather than re-derived per caller. `createChannelRunQueue` shares one run-state machine across all queue keys and `KeyedAsyncQueue` runs unrelated keys concurrently, so `activeRuns` routinely exceeds 1; tracking the oldest active run rather than a busy-streak start keeps a continuously busy account healthy while still catching a single hung run. Legitimate busy behavior is preserved: short, active, and overlapping runs stay healthy, and snapshots without a start time fall back to the previous `lastRunActivityAt` behavior. `onRunEnd` now takes the run handle returned by `onRunStart`; the only in-repo caller, `createChannelRunQueue`, is migrated in this same commit, and typed plugin consumers get a compile error rather than silent breakage. Restoring a no-argument `onRunEnd` overload was deliberately avoided because it would reintroduce the counter-decrement accounting this change removes and split run tracking across two paths. The 25 minute ceiling is the pre-existing `BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS` constant; this change only makes it reachable, so a single run in flight past it is now treated as stuck by design. This is distinct from PR #96198, which fixes the same class of heartbeat-hides-stuck bug in the agent diagnostic stuck-session detector (`src/agents/*`, `src/logging/diagnostic-run-activity.ts`), a different subsystem that does not touch channel health.

## User Impact

Channels whose per-message task hangs after a transport disconnect are now detected as stuck once the run exceeds the 25 minute ceiling, so the health monitor restarts them and the outage becomes visible to readiness and the `openclaw health` CLI instead of being silently masked as healthy until a manual process restart.

## Evidence

- New regression test in `src/gateway/channel-health-policy.test.ts`: a disconnected channel with a run in flight longer than the threshold and a fresh heartbeat now evaluates to `{ healthy: false, reason: "stuck" }`. Fails on pristine `main` (returns `busy`), passes with this patch. A companion case keeps a short-lived run `busy`.

target.title: Draft: add commands list and inspect inventory
target.body:
## Summary

Adds a read-only operator/developer command inventory:

```text
openclaw commands list [--json|--markdown] [--plugin-descriptors]
openclaw commands inspect <command-path...> [--json|--markdown] [--plugin-descriptors]
```

This is the recommended initial implementation from [Command Catalog RFC #32](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/32). It joins command information OpenClaw already owns so compliance, diagnostics, documentation, policy tooling, and future scoped prompt consumers do not each rebuild the same registry joins.

## Scope

`commands list` joins existing command-owned sources:

- static CLI descriptors
- command routes and routed operations
- the current Commander tree
- opt-in plugin CLI descriptors
- caller-supplied node command declarations

`commands inspect` hydrates the requested lazy core/sub-CLI group, resolves runtime aliases, and joins exact command records with inherited route and routed-operation metadata.

This draft does not add ownerless tool adapters, aggregate audit/test/summary commands, prompt generation, generated docs, or a new execution path. Node records are supported in the object model but no live `node.list` / `node.describe` bridge is claimed yet.

## Plugin contract and failure behavior

Plugin descriptors may optionally report `effectProfile`, `commandExposure`, and `hidden`. Their values, defaults, and non-enforcement semantics are documented in `docs/plugins/sdk-overview.md` with an external-plugin example.

When `--plugin-descriptors` is requested, loader exceptions or error-level plugin diagnostics now fail the command. They cannot produce an apparently valid incomplete inventory. Warnings remain visible without invalidating successful results.

## Existing Gateway surface

OpenClaw already has Gateway RPC `commands.list` for agent-facing chat/native/skill/plugin commands. This CLI adds an operator/developer inventory; it does not replace or change the Gateway RPC. Future convergence remains an explicit RFC decision.

## Review layers

- [PR1: commands list](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/24)
- [PR2: commands inspect and ClawSweeper hardening](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/25)
- [Optional PR3: scoped prompt projection](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/26)

## Real behavior proof

Exact head: `90a7b1ca2b`

Core-only inventory, using an isolated state directory:

```text
schemaVersion=1
commandDescriptors=61
runtimeCommands=26
pluginCommands=0
```

Opt-in plugin inventory, also isolated:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"commandDescriptors":61,"runtimeCommands":26,"pluginCommands":3,"pluginIds":"browser:browser,canvas:nodes canvas,memory-core:memory"}
```

```json
{"exitCode":1,"stdoutBytes":0,"errorMatched":true}
```

The failure fixture throws during plugin registration. The command emits no JSON document and exits nonzero with `Failed to load plugin CLI descriptor metadata` on stderr.

## Validation

- 44 focused inventory tests from the promoted PR1+PR2 stack
- latest hardening rerun: 10 focused CLI/metadata tests passed
- source execution proved core-only, plugin-enabled, and plugin-failure paths
- `git diff --check`
- clean final Codex review after the ClawSweeper fixes

The full local core TypeScript runner did not complete within two five-minute attempts on this worktree; it emitted no diagnostics. Focused Vitest compilation and runtime source execution passed.

## Feedback requested

Is `openclaw commands` the right initial public surface, with broader consumers added only after the command inventory contract is accepted?

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

## What Problem This Solves

Configured browser-node display names could fail to resolve when the selector and the connected node used canonically equivalent Unicode text, such as NFC `Café` versus NFD `Cafe` + U+0301. Browser routing also had a second matcher whose behavior could drift from the shared node resolver.

The fix must preserve the shipped browser-only compact selector contract (`MacStudio` matching `Mac Studio`) without making separator-insensitive matching a global node-selection rule.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared node matcher now normalizes names to NFC, handles Unicode letters, numbers, and meaningful combining marks, and strips only emoji decoration components that should not distinguish node names. Exact normalized display-name matches keep priority over compact matches.

Compact display-name matching is an explicit lower-priority option used only by the Gateway browser request path and the agent browser tool. The obsolete browser-specific matcher is deleted so both browser entry points share one implementation while non-browser node resolution keeps its existing stricter behavior.

## User Impact

Users can configure a browser node with composed Unicode text and still connect a node whose display name uses the equivalent decomposed form. CJK and combining-script names retain their meaningful marks, emoji variation/keycap decoration does not create false mismatches, exact matches win, and existing compact browser selectors continue to work.

Release-note context: browser node selection now resolves canonically equivalent Unicode display names consistently while keeping separator-insensitive compatibility scoped to browser selectors. Thanks @qingminglong.

target.title: fix(gateway): enforce plugin-ownership check in sessions.patch
target.body:
Closes #103077.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an in-process plugin-runtime caller could use `sessions.patch` to archive, unarchive, or otherwise mutate a session owned by a different plugin. `sessions.delete` already rejects cross-plugin cleanup, but `sessions.patch` performed the mutation with no ownership check.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing `rejectPluginRuntimeDeleteMismatch` helper in `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions.ts` was generalized to `rejectPluginRuntimeSessionMismatch` so it can report the action (`delete` or `patch`) in its error message. `sessions.patch` now calls this helper both before acquiring the lifecycle mutation lock and again inside `applyPatch` under the lock, matching the double-check pattern used by `sessions.delete`.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:**
1. `sessions.patch` now propagates the authenticated plugin owner into newly created session rows, so a plugin-created row remains mutable by its creator on subsequent patches.
2. Plugin-runtime callers now fail closed on legacy ownerless rows. Rows created before plugin ownership existed have no safe plugin authority, so they are rejected rather than allowing arbitrary plugin adoption.

## User Impact

Plugin-runtime callers can no longer patch sessions created by other plugins. Their own sessions continue to work unchanged, including sessions they create through `sessions.patch`. Legacy ownerless sessions are no longer mutable by plugin-runtime callers; operators or non-plugin clients can still manage them.

## Evidence

- Added regression test `sessions.patch limits plugin-runtime mutations to sessions owned by that plugin` in `src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts`. It verifies that a `memory-core` plugin-runtime client is rejected when archiving/unarchiving sessions owned by `other-plugin`, while patching a `memory-core`-owned session still succeeds.
- Added regression test `sessions.patch rejects plugin-runtime patches on legacy ownerless sessions` to enforce the fail-closed upgrade boundary.
- Added regression test `sessions.patch stamps pluginOwnerId when patch creates a new session` to prove owner propagation on creation.
- Added unit coverage in `src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` for `pluginOwnerId` stamping behavior.
- Focused local run:
  - `pnpm test src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` → 260 passed across gateway-core/gateway-server/gateway-client/gateway-methods shards.
  - `pnpm test src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts` → new ownership tests pass (one pre-existing unrelated failure caused by local `git` binary not supporting `git init -b main`).
- `oxlint` and `oxfmt` clean on changed files.

## Real behavior proof

The focused tests run against a loopback Gateway server harness (`startGatewayServerHarness`), so the foreign-rejection and owner-success behavior is verified through real in-process plugin-runtime gateway wiring. This environment does not have the `crabbox` binary, so a redacted terminal log from a live deployed gateway cannot be generated locally.

target.title: fix(gateway): bound busy channel health by real run age
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`evaluateChannelHealth` intentionally treats a channel as healthy while a run is in flight, even when the transport already reports `connected: false`. That busy override is meant to be bounded by a 25 minute stale ceiling, but the ceiling is measured from `lastRunActivityAt`, which the run-state heartbeat refreshes every 60 seconds for as long as any run is active.

If a per-message task hangs forever, for example a channel send blocking on a half-open or dead socket with no send timeout after the transport disconnected, `onRunEnd` never fires, the heartbeat keeps ticking, and `lastRunActivityAt` never ages past roughly 60 seconds. The `>= 25min` stuck branch, the only escape from busy-overrides-disconnected, becomes permanently unreachable. The account is then reported healthy forever by the channel health monitor (`if (health.healthy) continue`), the readiness probe (`src/gateway/server/readiness.ts`), and the `openclaw health` CLI (`src/commands/health.ts`). No restart fires and no operator-visible signal appears until the process is restarted. Transport disconnects mid-send with no send timeout are a normal production failure mode.

## Why This Change Was Made

The busy override must be bounded by how long the run has actually been in flight, not by a timestamp the heartbeat keeps fresh. A single hung run must eventually breach the stale ceiling.

Root cause, `src/gateway/channel-health-policy.ts` busy branch (before):

```ts
const runActivityAge =
  lastRunActivityAt == null
    ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
    : Math.max(0, policy.now - lastRunActivityAt);
if (runActivityAge < BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS) {
  return { healthy: true, reason: "busy" };
}
return { healthy: false, reason: "stuck" };
```

`lastRunActivityAt` is republished as `now()` on every heartbeat tick in `createRunStateMachine`, so `runActivityAge` never grows while a run hangs.

Fix. `createRunStateMachine` now tracks each in-flight run's start time keyed by an opaque run handle returned from `onRunStart` and passed back to `onRunEnd`, and publishes the oldest still-active run's start as `activeRunStartedAt`. When the oldest run ends the reported start advances to the next-oldest, and it clears when no run is active. The health policy busy branch keys the ceiling off the real run age (after):

```ts
const runStartAge =
  activeRunStartedAt == null ? null : Math.max(0, policy.now - activeRunStartedAt);
const runActivityAge =
  lastRunActivityAt == null ? null : Math.max(0, policy.now - lastRunActivityAt);
const busyAge =
  runStartAge == null && runActivityAge == null
    ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
    : Math.max(runStartAge ?? 0, runActivityAge ?? 0);
if (busyAge < BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS) {
  return { healthy: true, reason: "busy" };
}
return { healthy: false, reason: "stuck" };
```

Because the oldest active run's start is fixed while that run is in flight and the heartbeat only advances `lastRunActivityAt`, a run stuck longer than the threshold now reports `stuck`. Because the reported start is the oldest active run and advances as runs complete, a channel churning through many short overlapping runs stays healthy; only a genuinely hung run breaches the ceiling. The `activeRunStartedAt` field flows through the same run-state to snapshot path as `lastRunActivityAt` (`run-state-machine.ts` publish, `account-snapshot-fields.ts` read, `types.core.ts` snapshot type), so all three consumers of `evaluateChannelHealth` (monitor, readiness, CLI) get the corrected verdict.

## Why This Is The Right Boundary

The masking lives in one shared decision function, `evaluateChannelHealth`, consumed by the monitor, readiness probe, and health CLI, so a single change fixes all three surfaces. The heartbeat that defeats the ceiling lives in `createRunStateMachine`, the one owner of run activity status, so the run-age fact is surfaced where it is produced rather than re-derived per caller. `createChannelRunQueue` shares one run-state machine across all queue keys and `KeyedAsyncQueue` runs unrelated keys concurrently, so `activeRuns` routinely exceeds 1; tracking the oldest active run rather than a busy-streak start keeps a continuously busy account healthy while still catching a single hung run. Legitimate busy behavior is preserved: short, active, and overlapping runs stay healthy, and snapshots without a start time fall back to the previous `lastRunActivityAt` behavior. `onRunEnd` now takes the run handle returned by `onRunStart`; the only in-repo caller, `createChannelRunQueue`, is migrated in this same commit, and typed plugin consumers get a compile error rather than silent breakage. Restoring a no-argument `onRunEnd` overload was deliberately avoided because it would reintroduce the counter-decrement accounting this change removes and split run tracking across two paths. The 25 minute ceiling is the pre-existing `BUSY_ACTIVITY_STALE_THRESHOLD_MS` constant; this change only makes it reachable, so a single run in flight past it is now treated as stuck by design. This is distinct from PR #96198, which fixes the same class of heartbeat-hides-stuck bug in the agent diagnostic stuck-session detector (`src/agents/*`, `src/logging/diagnostic-run-activity.ts`), a different subsystem that does not touch channel health.

## User Impact

Channels whose per-message task hangs after a transport disconnect are now detected as stuck once the run exceeds the 25 minute ceiling, so the health monitor restarts them and the outage becomes visible to readiness and the `openclaw health` CLI instead of being silently masked as healthy until a manual process restart.

## Evidence

- New regression test in `src/gateway/channel-health-policy.test.ts`: a disconnected channel with a run in flight longer than the threshold and a fresh heartbeat now evaluates to `{ healthy: false, reason: "stuck" }`. Fails on pristine `main` (returns `busy`), passes with this patch. A companion case keeps a short-lived run `busy`.
- New tests in `src/channels/run-state-machine.test.ts`: across 26 minutes of heartbeat ticks `activeRunStartedAt` stays fixed at the run start while `lastRunActivityAt` advances; and when an older run ends while a newer run is still active the reported start advances to the next-oldest run, so overlapping short runs do not accumulate false age.
- Verification commands (from a deps-enabled checkout):
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/channel-health-policy.test.ts src/channels/run-state-machine.test.ts` passes on this patch.
  - Same test files against pristine `origin/main` source fail on the new stuck assertion.
  - `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs`, `oxfmt --check`, and `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs` (core and core-test) all clean on the changed files.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: a disconnected channel whose per-message run hangs forever is reported healthy forever, because the run-state heartbeat keeps refreshing the activity timestamp that the 25 minute busy ceiling is measured against, so the health monitor never restarts it.
Real environment tested: drove the real periodic health monitor loop from `startChannelHealthMonitor` (`src/gateway/channel-health-monitor.ts`) over the real `evaluateChannelHealth` (`src/gateway/channel-health-policy.ts`) fed by a live `createRunStateMachine` (`src/channels/run-state-machine.ts`) with its real `setInterval` heartbeat, on real wall-clock (`Date.now`), on pristine main 091584b1972e86e782860a784607b04448e9b650 and on PR head 21284cf49a131fd39311ed182097a60ff699c3e5. Only the channel transport was stubbed, at the narrowest seam (the `ChannelManager` the monitor calls), so the monitor's real restart recovery path stays observable. Executed on a remote Crabbox AWS lease (c7a.xlarge, eu-west-1, lease cbx_452e9479c6de), not on the author machine. The 25 minute busy ceiling and the 60 second heartbeat were both scaled down 300x (to 5 seconds and 200 milliseconds) so a genuinely hung run breaches the ceiling in seconds of real elapsed time rather than 26 minutes; nothing else was altered and both runs used identical scaling.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: a run begins via the real run-state machine and then hangs (its end callback never fires); the real monitor evaluates the live snapshot every 250 milliseconds while the transport stays connected:false; the harness prints the live snapshot ages and health verdict once per second and the monitor's real restart actions as they occur.
Evidence after fix:
```
# BEFORE (pristine main 091584b, run hung well past the scaled ceiling)
[health-monitor] started (interval: 0s, startup-grace: 0s, channel-connect-grace: 3600s)
t=1.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=n/a -> healthy=true reason=busy
t=5.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=n/a -> healthy=true reason=busy
t=7.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=n/a -> healthy=true reason=busy
SUMMARY monitorRestarts=0 finalVerdict=busy
# AFTER (PR head 21284cf, identical inputs, identical 300x scaling)
[health-monitor] started (interval: 0s, startup-grace: 0s, channel-connect-grace: 3600s)
t=1.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=1.0s -> healthy=true reason=busy
t=4.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=4.0s -> healthy=true reason=busy
t=5.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=5.0s -> healthy=false reason=stuck
[health-monitor] [telegram:acct-1] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stuck)
  RECOVERY stopChannel(telegram:acct-1)
  RECOVERY startChannel(telegram:acct-1) -> monitor restart #1
t=7.0s connected=false activeRuns=1 lastRunActivityAtAge=0.2s activeRunStartedAtAge=7.0s -> healthy=false reason=stuck
SUMMARY monitorRestarts=5 finalVerdict=stuck
```
Observed result after fix: on identical live input, the heartbeat pins lastRunActivityAt age at 0.2s in both runs, so BEFORE the channel stays healthy and busy for the whole hang and the monitor never restarts it (monitorRestarts=0); AFTER, the fixed activeRunStartedAt age grows until it breaches the ceiling, the verdict flips to unhealthy and stuck, and the real health monitor completes its restart recovery path (stopChannel then startChannel) five times over the window. The one value that moves from wrong to right is the health verdict for a hung disconnected channel, and with it the monitor's restart action.
What was not tested: no live provider socket was hung end to end; the hang was a real never-resolving run under the real heartbeat, and the transport was a stub at the ChannelManager seam. The busy ceiling and heartbeat were scaled 300x on real wall-clock so the breach happens in seconds; the unscaled 25 minute breach was not waited out. Full build not run; the change is not on a lazy or packaging boundary.

target.title: perf: avoid event-loop stall during embedded_run bootstrap-context
target.body:
## Summary

Fix event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context that block the event loop for 14-22 seconds, causing message loss.

### Root causes addressed

1. **Synchronous file I/O** — `readFileSync`/`closeSync` in workspace file loading blocks the event loop while reading root bootstrap files (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, etc.)
2. **Unbounded blocking glob walks** — `fs.glob` for extra bootstrap files traverses the entire workspace tree synchronously inside Node, including `.git`/`node_modules` directories, without yielding to the event loop
3. **Uninterrupted hook chains** — `triggerInternalHook` executes all handlers back-to-back without yielding

### Changes

**`src/agents/workspace.ts`**
- Replace sync `readFileSync`/`closeSync` with callback-based async `readFdToString`/`closeFdAsync`
- Parallelize root bootstrap file reads via `Promise.all` (previously serial `for` loop)
- Replace `fs.glob` with an async traversal walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries, so a sparse pattern like `**/AGENTS.md` over a large workspace never blocks the event loop. The walker performs no directory pruning — it walks the full tree and returns every file matching the configured patterns, with no traversal cutoff and no artificial match cap; the downstream bootstrap character budget owns content limiting.
- Preserve `fs.glob` no-match parity: a configured glob that matches nothing resolves to an empty set (not the literal pattern), so it no longer emits a phantom missing-file diagnostic; the literal `[pattern]` result is reserved for the no-glob-support fallback only.
- Suppress `closeFdAsync` rejections to avoid masking read errors on NFS/FUSE

**`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`** / **`src/hooks/internal-hook-dispatch.ts`**
- Keep the public `triggerInternalHook(event)` signature (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/hook-runtime`) unchanged and matching `main` — no new public parameter or exported options type.
- Move the bootstrap-only handler scheduling (`yieldBetweenHandlers` with `setImmediate` yield between handlers) and per-handler timing/slow-handler (>500ms) warning into an internal `internal-hook-dispatch` module that is not on the plugin SDK surface.

**`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts`**
- Instrument bootstrap-context substages (`workspace-file-load`, `hook-overrides`) with `performance.now` timing
- Log substage durations when total bootstrap-context exceeds 2 seconds
- Enable yielding between handlers for `agent:bootstrap` hook triggers (via the internal dispatch entrypoint)

**`src/agents/bootstrap-files.ts`** / **`src/agents/bootstrap-hooks.ts`**
- Keep the public `resolveBootstrapFilesForRun` params (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`) callback-free and matching `main`; route embedded-runner substage timing through an internal `resolveBootstrapFilesForRunWithTiming` variant kept off the SDK surface.
- Support the new async workspace file loading interface.

### Tests

- `workspace.test.ts` — 3 new tests for async fd read (happy path, cache hit, fd close on failure)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — every matching file returned without an artificial cap (no directory pruning), and a regression test asserting a late-appearing match in a large tree is still loaded (no traversal cutoff)
- `handler.test.ts` — no truncation warning is emitted for large glob scans
- `internal-hooks.test.ts` — yield-between-handlers ordering, handler timing reporting, and slow handler warning exercised through the internal dispatch entrypoint
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — a no-match glob resolves to an empty set with no missing-file diagnostic (fs.glob parity)

The public plugin SDK surface is unchanged: `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` exits 0 with no new package-exported entrypoints. All existing tests pass without modification.

### Performance impact

- Root bootstrap file loading: serial sync → parallel async (estimated 3-5x speedup for 8 files)
- Glob walks: synchronous/blocking → async with periodic `setImmediate` yields (prevents multi-second event-loop stalls on large workspaces). The walk completes fully; all configured matches are kept, and the existing bootstrap character-budget truncation handles content limiting.
- Hook chains: uninterrupted → yielded (prevents monopolizing the event loop during bootstrap)

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading caused by synchronous I/O and a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces, which blocks the loop and drops messages. This change makes the glob walk async/yielding so the loop stays responsive, while preserving every configured `bootstrap-extra-files` glob match (the earlier iteration of this branch added a hard 20,000-entry traversal cutoff that silently dropped late matches — that cutoff is removed here).
- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`, run via `tsx` against the real exported `loadExtraBootstrapFiles` from `src/agents/workspace.ts`. Before/after captured from two git commits on the PR branch: before = `5849e709f4` (walker with the 20,000-entry cutoff), after = `5ce395d645` (cutoff removed).
- **Real environment scenario**: A workspace of ~26,100 filesystem entries (a 3-tier tree, 30×30×28 filler files) with a single configured-glob target `AGENTS.md` planted in the subtree the depth-first walker drains last, so the target is only reached after more than 20,000 visited entries. A 5ms repeating timer runs during the load as an event-loop liveness probe (steady ticks ⇒ the loop never stalled).
- **Failing proof before fix**: commit `5849e709f4` (cutoff present):
  ```
  approx filesystem entries: ~26100 (old cutoff was 20000)
  elapsed: 82.9ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 16 (loop responsive)
  matched bootstrap files returned: 0
  deep AGENTS.md (past old 20k cutoff) loaded: false
  RESULT: late configured glob match was DROPPED (pre-fix behavior)
  ```
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  ```
  # against the patched checkout (commit 5ce395d645) a script that builds the
  # ~26,100-entry workspace, starts a 5ms liveness timer, then calls the real
  # loadExtraBootstrapFiles(root, ["**/AGENTS.md"]) and checks the deep match:
  npx tsx proof-live.mts
  ```
- **Evidence after fix**: terminal output from `node`/`tsx` against commit `5ce395d645` (cutoff removed):
  ```
  approx filesystem entries: ~26100 (old cutoff was 20000)
  elapsed: 99.4ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 20 (loop responsive)
  matched bootstrap files returned: 1
  deep AGENTS.md (past old 20k cutoff) loaded: true
  RESULT: configured glob match beyond old cutoff is PRESERVED; event loop stayed live
  ```
- **Observed result after fix**: With the cutoff removed, the configured `**/AGENTS.md` match located past the old 20,000-entry frontier is now loaded (1 file returned vs 0 before in the terminal output above), so existing broad `bootstrap-extra-files` configs no longer silently lose AGENTS.md/TOOLS.md context. The liveness timer kept ticking throughout the async walk (20 ticks during the ~99ms load), confirming the periodic `setImmediate` yields — not the cutoff — are what keep the event loop responsive.
- **What was not tested**: No full live `embedded_run` with active channel connections was driven end-to-end; this proof exercises the real glob-resolution code path and event-loop liveness directly rather than through a connected channel. The focused regression coverage lives in `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` and `handler.test.ts`.

Closes #87509

AI-assisted contribution.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using remote MCP servers would see repeated WARN-level startup noise when a tool schema used an informational, non-standard JSON Schema `format` such as `google-duration`.

## Why This Change Was Made

OpenClaw now strips only unknown schema `format` values before non-draft MCP schemas reach the SDK AJV validator. Known AJV formats such as `email`, `uri`, and date/time formats remain in place, so this removes the noisy warning without disabling standard format validation. Existing draft-2020-12 handling keeps its current format-stripping behavior.

## User Impact

Remote MCP servers with vendor-specific schema formats can load without polluting boot logs with duplicate warnings, while normal schema validation still catches invalid values for supported standard formats.

## Evidence

- Reproduced the underlying AJV behavior locally: compiling a schema with `format: "google-duration"` emits duplicate `unknown format` warnings while still validating successfully.
- Added a regression test proving `google-duration` no longer calls `console.warn` and that a known `email` format still rejects invalid input.

target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #103732.

`memory_search(corpus=sessions)` returned 0 hits — and unfiltered searches never surfaced session chunks — while `openclaw memory search` returned session results from the same index (reporter: 1133 indexed session chunks).

### Root cause

Only the tool path runs `filterMemorySearchHitsBySessionVisibility` (`extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts`); the CLI (`cli.runtime.ts`) returns raw `manager.search` results. Inside the filter, every hit's resolved session keys are already scoped to the requester's agent (`filterSessionKeysByScopedAgent`), but each key must then pass a `history`-action visibility guard whose **default `"tree"` visibility forbids every session that is not the requester or its descendant** (`src/plugin-sdk/session-visibility.ts` tree branch). A normal main-agent call (`agent:main:main`) therefore drops every historical `sessions/main/<uuid>` transcript — all of them.

### Change

`extensions/memory-core/src/session-search-visibility.ts`: same-agent hits from **authoritative** key resolutions (QMD artifact identity, exact live-stem matches, plain transcript stems) no longer require the per-key history guard — the agent scoping already applied is the boundary that matters for memory recall. Two protections are preserved deliberately:
- **sandboxed runs** keep the strict guard, so the spawned-subtree clamp still holds;
- **lossy QMD slug-fallback resolutions** keep the strict guard, so a slug cannot authorize the wrong transcript (existing regression `does not authorize QMD archived .md hits through lossy slug fallback` still passes).

## Verification

- New regressions (first one confirmed failing on main): same-agent hit under the default tree visibility is retained; the same hit under `sandboxed: true` is still dropped.
- `pnpm test extensions/memory-core` — full plugin suite passed (including all 728-line visibility suite + the lossy-slug security case).
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`, oxfmt — clean.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: memory_search tool returns 0 session hits despite an indexed sessions corpus; CLI works.
Real environment tested: the real `filterMemorySearchHitsBySessionVisibility` production filter through its dedicated test harness with a real combined session store shape (`agent:main:historic` transcript, requester `agent:main:main`, default visibility).
Exact steps or command run after this patch: `pnpm test extensions/memory-core`
Evidence after fix: the same-agent hit that main drops (tree forbid) is retained; sandboxed and lossy-slug paths still deny.
Observed result after fix: corpus=sessions recall returns same-agent transcripts, matching the CLI.
What was not tested: a live gateway with a populated QMD/sqlite index; the divergence is fully reproduced at the filter boundary that separates the tool path from the CLI path.

target.title: fix: preserve tool-result text across media fallback and context pressure
target.body:
Refs #99241

## What Problem This Solves

This PR covers the two interacting model-visible failure stages reported in #99241:

1. Provider serializers could turn an empty text-only tool result into `(see attached image)`, masking upstream text loss as a media result.
2. Under aggregate tool-result pressure, recovery could reduce or clear a freshly completed result before provider dispatch whenever runtime context, steering, or a follow-up message made that result non-trailing.

The July 9 report on this PR was correct for the earlier head: the provider/media patch removed the placeholder symptom but did not stop prompt projection from emptying fresh text. This updated head fixes both stages.

## Why This Change Was Made

The earlier beta fixes were important but incomplete:

- `v2026.7.1-beta.2` contains #97742 and #98955. They preserve structured text and protect the ordinary syntactically trailing fresh-result batch.
- That protection is trailing-only. A new result followed by runtime context, steering, or follow-up input is still a reachable non-trailing fresh result and could be selected before frozen history.
- The beta.3 line adds #100077 (budget scaling / compaction pressure) and #100272 (runtime-context carrier placement). Those mitigate pressure or change the tail shape, but neither establishes a general projection-freshness recovery invariant.

This update adopts the general fresh-projection invariant proposed in #99524, with credit to @snowzlmbot, and carries forward this PR's runtime-context regression coverage on current `main`.

In aggregate recovery, an unfrozen projection that appears after a frozen baseline is treated as fresh. Recovery now reduces ordinary eligible history first, then frozen history, and only then fresh non-trailing results. The existing trailing batch remains fully protected. If historical reductions cannot satisfy the hard cap, fresh results remain eligible as the final fallback, so the cap is still enforced.

For provider serialization, a new internal media-only fallback helper prevents empty text-only results from becoming image placeholders. The exported `describeToolResultMediaPlaceholder` behavior remains identical to current `main`, preserving its public Plugin SDK contract for mixed text/media callers.

## User Impact

Long-lived sessions with heavy `exec`, `read`, browser, or other tool traffic should keep the newest tool output model-readable across runtime-context, steering, and follow-up boundaries while older projected history is reduced first.

Media-only results retain a descriptive placeholder. Mixed text/media results preserve explicit text. No config change, migration, or new runtime option is required.

## Evidence

### Reproduction and focused coverage

- The live dist instrumentation in #99241 showed a 234-character fresh result selected as the only eligible entry, reduced to 69 characters, then cleared while 256,138 frozen characters remained.
- New regressions cover 234-character and 4,000-character sentinels followed by runtime-context, steering, and queued follow-up messages.
- A hard-cap regression proves fresh text is eventually reduced when frozen history alone cannot satisfy the budget.
- The existing real `convertToLlm` boundary regression still proves runtime-context carrier metadata survives provider conversion.

### Automated validation

- Focused provider, transport, serializer, and aggregate-truncation suite:
  - 10 files across 3 Vitest shards
  - 792 tests passed after the final merge from `upstream/main`
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs <15 changed files>`: passed.
- `oxfmt --check <15 changed files>`: passed.
- `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD`: passed.
- Clean-checkout build:
  - `OPENCLAW_BUILD_ALL_NO_PNPM=1 OPENCLAW_RUN_NODE_SKIP_DTS_BUILD=1 node scripts/build-all.mjs gatewayWatch`
  - passed.

### Real Gateway / model proof

A clean checkout containing only current OpenClaw plus this PR patch was run through a real local Gateway with `deepseek-v4-flash` and a 128K context window:

- 40 consecutive real `exec` tool calls in one session.
- 272,000 total characters of tool-result text.
- 40/40 unique sentinels were read and acknowledged by the model, from `H01` through `H40`.
- 14 compaction entries occurred; prompt usage crossed pressure and compacted during the run without losing the fresh sentinel.

This is direct Gateway/provider long-session proof. Browser UI proof is not included in this update.

### Codex autoreview

Repository autoreview was run repeatedly with Codex (`gpt-5.5`, high reasoning):

- One accepted finding identified a mixed text/media regression risk; the implementation was changed to use a non-exported media-only serializer helper.
- A later public-helper finding was rejected after direct comparison with `upstream/main`: the exported helper is unchanged, and the internal helper is not exported through the Plugin SDK.
- No accepted or actionable findings remain.

AI-assisted: reproduction analysis, implementation, validation, and final review were performed with Codex.

target.title: fix: severe per-message slowdown when commands.ownerAllowFrom has thousands of entries
target.body:
Closes #50289

## What Problem This Solves

Gateways with large `commands.ownerAllowFrom` lists can spend 15–27 seconds processing each message and emit `lane wait exceeded` warnings. The reporter has 9,282 entries. Command authorization repeatedly trimmed, parsed, channel-filtered, and plugin-formatted the complete list, then used linear array membership checks. That work ran for every inbound message and scaled with the configured list size.

The same behavior is present in the current release and on `main`. PR #103523 improves membership lookup but still constructs the prepared data on every message, so it does not remove the dominant repeated list transformation.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change prepares each configured allow-from array once and carries those facts through the existing command-authorization owner boundary:

- parsed entries and channel filtering;
- plugin-formatted owner and command lists;
- wildcard state; and
- membership `Set`s.

The cache is deliberately scoped by the raw array, `OpenClawConfig` identity, actual plugin implementation identity, provider, account, and owner/command formatting mode. A config reload or plugin-registry replacement therefore cannot reuse stale formatted values. Per-message `ctx.OwnerAllowFrom` overrides retain their existing precedence.

This is the best-fit fix because it removes repeated request-time discovery at the authorization boundary instead of adding another per-message cache or only replacing `.includes`. The shipped mutable `CommandAuthorization.ownerList` SDK shape is preserved with a defensive copy at the public boundary, so callers cannot mutate cached authorization state. That compatibility copy and sender-candidate normalization still run per call; the claim is therefore that the expensive configured-list transformation is reused, not that every operation is strictly O(1).

## User Impact

With a 10,000-entry `ownerAllowFrom`, the production-entry-point harness improved from **17.4 ms/message to 0.009 ms/message** (about 1,900×) while preserving owner, channel-prefix, wildcard, override, and command-allowlist behavior. Small configurations retain the same authorization semantics.

The change is internal to command authorization. It adds no config, migration, protocol, or Plugin SDK surface.

## Evidence

The real-behavior harness calls `resolveCommandAuthorization` with 10,000 mixed channel-prefixed, numeric, and whitespace-padded entries, plus a Discord-shaped plugin formatter.

**Before (`main`):**

```text
[PASS] listed sender is owner
[PASS] unlisted sender is not owner
[PASS] telegram-prefixed entry does not authorize a discord sender
timing: 200 messages, 10000 entries -> 3482 ms total, 17.408 ms/message
[FAIL] authorization stays under 1 ms/message
```

**After (this branch):**

```text
[PASS] listed sender is owner
[PASS] unlisted sender is not owner
[PASS] telegram-prefixed entry does not authorize a discord sender
timing: 200 messages, 10000 entries -> 2 ms total, 0.009 ms/message
[PASS] authorization stays under 1 ms/message
```

`src/auto-reply/command-auth.prepared.test.ts` adds 14 regression tests covering:

- channel-prefixed, numeric, whitespace-padded, cross-channel, and unlisted entries;
- compile-once behavior with a 5,000-entry list;
- provider and account-sensitive formatting;
- shared-array isolation across config identities;
- shared config/array isolation across plugin-registry replacements with the same plugin ID;
- mutation isolation for the SDK-facing `ownerList`;
- `ctx.OwnerAllowFrom` precedence; and
- provider-specific and global `commands.allowFrom` behavior.

Existing focused authorization, Plugin SDK, command-control, stop-target, and subagent-routing suites remain in the CI selection. Repository formatting and `git diff --check` pass. Two independent Codex autoreviews (hardening diff and full PR branch) reported no actionable findings.

[Secretless fork-PR CI run 29120968934](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29120968934) on exact head `9bb38e94dfd` passed production types, test types, every Node test shard, build artifacts, both QA smoke profiles, channel/plugin contracts, dependency guards, and security-fast. Its only failures are current-`main` baselines outside this diff: lint errors in `queue.drain-restart.test.ts` and `server.chat.gateway-server-chat.test.ts`, plus an ACP/agents Madge cycle. The immediately preceding [`main` run 29119824112](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29119824112) failed the same two jobs.

Known proof gap: the contributor-safe AWS Crabbox broker rejected this non-member account before allocating a lease, so no credential-hydrated Testbox was used. The pushed head was instead validated by the repository's secretless fork-PR CI above. A live 9k-user channel deployment was not available; the benchmark uses the production authorization entry point with the bundled Discord formatter's normalization shape. Config-file parsing reported in #50289 is a separate load-time surface and remains out of scope.

---

This PR is AI-assisted (Claude Opus and Codex, human-operated). The final branch was independently reviewed after the cache-lifecycle and SDK-mutation regressions were added.

target.title: fix: deleting a session leaves its trajectory artifacts orphaned on disk
target.body:
Closes #89200

> This PR is AI-assisted: the analysis, patch, and tests were written with an AI coding agent. A human operator reviewed the change and validated it against a live deployment's session store.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where deleting a session (dashboard delete or the `sessions.delete` RPC) leaves its trajectory artifacts orphaned on disk forever. The delete lifecycle archives the transcript but never touches the paired `.trajectory.jsonl` / `.trajectory-path.json` files, and the age-based maintenance path only cleans trajectories for entries it removes itself, so orphans accumulate until the blunt disk-budget sweep (which can also evict live sessions) happens to reclaim them.

## Why This Change Was Made

`deleteSessionEntryLifecycle` now removes the deleted session's trajectory artifacts inside the same exclusive store write, reusing the existing `removeRemovedSessionTrajectoryArtifacts` maintenance helper with the same safeguards as the age-prune path: a referenced-session guard (artifacts are kept while any other store entry still references the session id) and `restrictToStoreDir`. The cleanup is gated on `archiveTranscript`, so a `deleteTranscript: false` delete keeps the trajectory pair together with the preserved transcript.

## User Impact

Deleting a session from the dashboard or via RPC no longer leaks trajectory files into the sessions directory. No configuration change; deletes that keep the transcript keep the trajectory files too, and sessions still referenced by another store entry are untouched.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.runtime-config.config.ts src/config/sessions/store.session-lifecycle-mutation.test.ts src/config/sessions/artifacts.test.ts src/config/sessions/store.pruning.test.ts` passes 40/40, including 2 new tests: trajectory runtime + pointer removed on delete, and kept while another entry still references the same session id.
- Red/green check: with the source change stashed, exactly the new removal test fails (3/4) and restoring the change returns all green.
- Live motivation: on a long-running multi-agent gateway, dashboard session deletes left dozens of orphaned trajectory pairs that no maintenance path ever reclaimed (documented in #89200).
- Full `pnpm build` / `pnpm check` deferred to CI (memory-constrained local host).

## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

## Tests and validation

```text

## Summary
- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text
- `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`, `memory.md`, `system-prompt.md`
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`
- `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Installed OpenClaw `2026.5.20` (npm global, current `latest` published build, ahead of the `acf265d` base this PR branches from), against the live workspace `~/.openclaw/workspace-moku` used by the gateway. Agent `main`, local embedding provider, per-agent SQLite memory store at `~/.openclaw/memory/main.sqlite`. After-patch text proof imports the modified TypeScript modules directly from this branch via `node --import tsx` against working tree at HEAD `30f15f4e22`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

Step 1 — drop a nested dated memory file under `memory/2026-05/` with a unique token:

```
cat > ~/.openclaw/workspace-moku/memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md <<'EOF'
Recursive memory search proof.
Unique token for PR 85899 smoke test: PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY
This file lives at memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md
EOF
```

Step 2 — reindex the live agent's memory store:

```
openclaw memory index
```

Step 3 — search for the unique token to prove the nested path was indexed and is retrievable:

```
openclaw memory search "PROOFTOKEN_QXZ7K_NESTED_RECURSIVE_MEMORY" --max-results 3
```

Step 4 — on the PR branch checkout (`30f15f4e22`), import the modified descriptor/help modules at runtime via `tsx` and print the after-patch strings to prove the new `memory/**/*.md` wording is observable from a real runtime call site (not just the diff):

```
node --import tsx _proof-c.mjs   # imports FIELD_HELP and buildPromptSection from this branch
```

**After-fix evidence**: Terminal output from the installed `openclaw 2026.5.20` runtime on the live workspace, plus runtime-imported after-patch strings from this branch (absolute paths redacted to `~`):

```
$ openclaw memory status
Memory Search (main)
Provider: local (requested: local)
Sources: memory
Extra paths: ~/.openclaw/shared-memory
Indexed: 105/105 files . 933 chunks
Workspace: ~/.openclaw/workspace-moku
By source:

```

Memory index updated (main).

[node-llama-cpp] ... falling back to using no GPU

```

**Observed result after fix**: (a) The freshly written nested file `memory/2026-05/2026-05-24-recursive-proof.md` (two levels deep under `memory/`) was indexed by `openclaw memory index` and returned as the top match (score `0.812`) for the unique token. **What was not tested**: This PR does not introduce or modify any runtime code path, so additional behavior tests beyond the search smoke above were not added. The recursive walk itself (`collectMemoryFilesFromDir`) is already covered by upstream tests under `packages/memory-host-sdk/`.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
